title: Ways to Spell a Word by Deleting
statement:
You get a string s and a shorter word t. Delete some characters of s (keeping the rest in order) so that what remains is exactly t.

Count the ways to do it. Two ways are different if they keep a different set of positions of s, even when the kept letters are the same. The count can be astronomically large, so return it modulo 1 000 000 007.

examples.why: Positions (0, 1), (0, 3) and (2, 3). Multiplying 2 x's by 2 y's gives 4, but the y at 1 cannot follow the x at 2.
Both letters are there, but in the wrong order.
Any 2 of the 4 positions. Every result is the same string "aa", but positions are what is counted.

constraints: s and t hold lowercase English letters
hints: Look at the last character of s. Either it is deleted, or it is kept as the last character of t, which is only possible if they are equal.
Let dp[i][j] be the number of ways to spell t[0..j) from s[0..i). Deleting s[i−1] leaves dp[i−1][j]; using it for t[j−1] leaves dp[i−1][j−1]. What is dp[i][0]?

dp[i][j] = dp[i−1][j] + (s[i−1] == t[j−1] ? dp[i−1][j−1] : 0), with dp[i][0] = 1 and dp[0][j > 0] = 0. Take the modulo after every addition. With one row, loop j downward so row[j−1] still holds the previous row's value.

explain.intuition:
Let dp[i][j] be the number of ways to spell the first j letters of t using only the first i letters of s. Read the recurrence off the last decision, about s[i−1]. Either it is deleted, and all of t[0..j) must come from s[0..i−1): dp[i−1][j] ways. Or it is kept as the final letter t[j−1], which requires s[i−1] == t[j−1], and the rest of t must come from earlier: dp[i−1][j−1] ways. Those two groups of choices never overlap, so add them.

The base cases carry the meaning. Spelling the empty word is always possible in exactly one way (delete everything), so dp[i][0] = 1. A non-empty word cannot come from an empty prefix, so dp[0][j] = 0. Counts double easily (every extra a in a string of as grows them like binomials), so apply the modulo after each addition. With values kept below about 2·10⁹, plain JavaScript numbers stay exact.
steps: For each character c of s in order:
For j from t.length down to 1: if c == t[j−1], set row[j] = (row[j] + row[j−1]) % MOD. Going downward means row[j−1] is still the value from before c, so c is used at most once per spelling.
pitfalls: Counting distinct resulting strings, or multiplying letter counts. Positions are counted, and order matters: the first example is 3, not 1 and not 4.
Looping j upward in the one-row version. A single a of s could then fill both letters of "aa", so s = "a", t = "aa" would give 1 instead of 0.
Applying the modulo only at the end. The intermediate counts overflow 64-bit integers, and JavaScript numbers lose exactness above 2⁵³.

solutions.title: Recursion: keep or delete each letter
solutions.idea: For each letter of s, either skip it, or use it for the next letter of t when they match. Every way to spell t is one leaf of the recursion, so the time grows with the answer itself.

solutions.title: Table over both prefixes
solutions.idea: dp[i][j] = dp[i−1][j] (delete s[i−1]) + dp[i−1][j−1] if s[i−1] == t[j−1] (keep it), modulo after every step.

solutions.title: One row, updated right to left
solutions.idea: Row i only reads row i − 1 at j and j − 1. Updating j from high to low keeps row[j − 1] at its old value.

followups: Return the exact count as a big integer instead of a residue. What does that cost?
Many different words t are asked against the same long s. What could you precompute?
Count distinct strings of length k that are subsequences of s, instead of position sets.
